Saul Loeb | Afp | Getty Images Four of the largest U.S. banks are reporting third-quarter results before the market opens on Tuesday: JPMorgan Chase , Wells Fargo and Goldman Sachs are first out of the gates. The quarter was dominated by headlines around artificial intelligence, IPO uncertainty, high fuel prices and rising borrowing costs. All four reports on Tuesday are due by 8 a.m. ET, and executives from each of the banks will be addressing those topics and more during earnings calls between 8:30 a.m. and 11 a.m. ET. Fixed income trading of $5.4 billion was about $550 million below the StreetAccount estimate. Companywide expenses of $27.3 billion were about $90 million worse than expected. That's not a huge miss, but it shows that costs grew by 12% year over year in a quarter where revenue grew by 8%, a dynamic investors and analysts usually don't love. That 8% revenue growth rate is a real slowdown compared to the 27% surge of the second quarter, where equities trading and dealmaking exceeded expectations. Lastly, the securities write-off of $658 million pretax cut EPS by 18 cents, though at least some analysts are likely to exclude that figure from their assessment of the quarter. — Hugh Son 39 Min Ago JPMorgan stock turns positive JPMorgan shares are higher as of about 7:20 a.m. ET after initially falling on an earnings miss. Dimon gives few clues as to why his bank missed third-quarter estimates, saying JPMorgan "reported another quarter of strong results." But there is one sign that corporations and institutional investors may have taken a more "risk off" approach as the quarter progressed: In the firm's Wall Street division, Dimon noted that trading and investment banking activity "did moderate somewhat during the quarter." headlines.article_text: Micron, SK Hynix, Samsung Electronics, ASML shares: tech stocks fall Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Technology stocks tumbled Tuesday as a sell-off in U.S. semiconductor shares spilled into Asian and European markets. China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, reported progress on a new chip structure, intensifying chip competition. Intel and Broadcom CEOs have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the artificial intelligence boom. In this article 9984.T-JP ASML STM IFX-DE SKHY Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Samuel Boivin | Nurphoto | Getty Images Technology stocks fell Tuesday, extending a sell-off sparked by worries over artificial intelligence financing and intensifying competition. Memory chip giant Micron was down around 3.8% in U.S. premarket trading. Other memory-related stocks such as SanDisk , Seagate and Western Digital were all sharply lower. The slide, which follows declines on Wall Street on Monday, comes as investors assessed intensifying competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT . Micron shares year-to-date. Over the weekend , CXMT announced significant progress in developing a new chip architecture, designed to increase memory density by packing more data into a smaller space. CXMT is China's leading rival to the likes of Micron and South Korean heavyweights SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics. Analysts broadly see CXMT as trailing the U.S. and South Korean memory leaders, which means any advancement from the Chinese firm could add more competition to the market leaders. "Investors are jittery and looking for excuses to take profit on AI-related stocks that have outperformed this year, especially memory stocks," said UBP's senior equity advisor Vey-Sern Ling. "In reality, while the Chinese memory makers can potentially become a threat to global demand-supply balance over time, in the short run they continue to face technology hurdles, especially for more advanced memory like HBM," Ling told CNBC via email. CXMT shares closed 2.8% lower in Shanghai. Global tech stocks slump Adding fuel to the sell-off was a post by Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, who said China has the ability to scale production once it figures out how to manufacture something. "When China figures out how to manufacture a product, their ability to scale is often greater than the rest of the world combined," Musk said on Monday. European chip stocks also sank in early morning trade, with semiconductor equipment maker ASML down 3.3%, and STMicroelectronics and German chip maker Infineon both down 5%. Dutch firms BE Semiconductor and ASM International were both around 4% lower at the open. Shares of South Korean chip giant SK Hynix, a leading supplier of high-bandwidth memory chips used in artificial intelligence applications, plunged more than 10%, while rival Samsung Electronics shed 7.4% — both hitting their lowest levels since August. SK Hynix's U.S.-listed stock was down around 5% in premarket trading. watch now VIDEO 4:30 04:30 Tech shakedown spreads as U.S. heavyweights face fresh selling Squawk Box Europe In Japan, shares of tech-focused investment giant SoftBank Group sank 8.5%. The group, which has significant exposure to the global AI industry through its huge investment in OpenAI, led a broader retreat in Japanese semiconductor and electronics shares. Tokyo Electron , a major supplier of chipmaking equipment, dropped 7.2%, while Advantest , which makes semiconductor testing equipment, declined 2.9%. Other Japanese technology stocks also came under pressure. Lasertec fell over 5%, Disco lost 4.7% and Renesas Electronics shed 5.9%. The declines followed a weak session for technology stocks on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.44% on Monday. U.S. memory chipmaker Micron Technology slid 3.9% as 'Vulnerable' AI sentiment? Phillip Wool, chief market strategist at Rayliant Global Advisors, said CXMT's breakthrough marked a significant milestone for Chinese chipmakers , demonstrating their ability to overcome technology restrictions and potentially challenge established players sooner than expected. But he cautioned that the market reaction appeared disproportionate to the immediate competitive threat, given that CXMT has yet to demonstrate large-scale production and continues to lag Samsung and SK Hynix in market share. "More importantly, we're not even talking about HBM here, and the Korean chipmakers are still unquestionably dominating that space, with very little threat at all from the likes of CXMT or anyone else for the foreseeable future," Wool said. He said the sharp sell-off reflected broader anxiety over the AI trade rather than a fundamental shift in the competitive landscape. "I read that more as a sign of how vulnerable AI sentiment is at this moment," Wool said, warning that volatility could persist as investors reassess chip demand and how long semiconductor manufacturers can sustain their pricing power. The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the AI boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply. Investors are also looking ahead to a busy week of corporate earnings and U.S. inflation data, which could provide fresh clues on the outlook for interest rates that often have an inverse correlation with growth stocks. Shares fell more than 2% before the bell. The company posted third-quarter revenue of $25.4 billion, above analysts' average estimate of $25.28 billion, according to LSEG data. Adjusted earnings of $2.59 per share also topped Wall Street expectations of $2.54. Pharmaceutical sales jumped 7.7% to $16.76 billion. Medical technology division sales rose only 2.5% to $8.6 billion overall. Outside the U.S., the division's sales were essentially flat. J&J Chief Financial Officer Joe Wolk said in an interview that the Mideast conflict, austerity measures in Europe, and pricing in China continued to weigh on international results, "but maybe in a little bit more pronounced way." He said the Mideast conflict, which has led to soaring fuel costs at home and abroad, has yet to impact the company's costs, but has hurt sales in the region. "These are countries that still value and actually want premium healthcare systems, think Kuwait, UAE, Saudi Arabia. They pride themselves on having solid healthcare, very good healthcare," Wolk said. "But their budgets now are being resourced and allocated towards defense." Sales of its Abiomed heart pump business also remained slow after a UK study earlier this year raised questions about using Impella pumps during certain high-risk ​coronary procedures. The company had late last year said it intended to separate its orthopedics unit. J&J is leaning toward spinning out its hips-and-knees business, Wolk told the Wall Street Journal. Tremfya sales rose 68% to $2.4 billion, beating analysts' estimates of about $2.19 billion, while Stelara sales, which face generic competition, fell 54% to $716 million, still well above Wall Street expectations of $591 million. Tremfya has increasingly replaced lost Stelara revenue following recent approvals in inflammatory bowel diseases. Sales of blood cancer treatment Darzalex rose about 16% to $4.24 billion, short of analyst expectations of $4.4 billion. The company raised its full-year sales forecast to about $101.2 billion at the midpoint, from $101.1 billion previously. It increased its adjusted earnings forecast range with a new midpoint of $11.10 per share, up from $11.04. J&J shares closed at $263.73 on Monday.
